k-accomplished.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>sheep</radical> climbs a <radical>road</radical>, its surface <radical>split</radical> into ruts of packed <radical>earth</radical>. The flock keeps stalling, but the last one clears the rise: the job is <kanji>accomplished</kanji>.
k-accomplished.reading_mnemonic: Tatsu is the drover who marks the top of every hill the same way: one slap on the gatepost and a barked 「<reading>たつ</reading>」 — done, next. He has said it at every gate between here and the coast. たつ means it is finished.

k-ancestor.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>altar</radical> stands on the left. Beside it, an <radical>eye</radical> lies flat above a line of <radical>ground</radical> — a portrait propped over the offerings. Somebody long dead looks back at you off that shelf: your <kanji>ancestor</kanji>.
k-ancestor.reading_mnemonic: So is the small catch of sound the incense makes when it takes light at the altar — 「<reading>そ</reading>」 — and for a second the eye in the portrait seems to move. One syllable, once a year, for the ancestor. そ.

k-breath.meaning_mnemonic: You jab a finger at your own <radical>self</radical> to answer for something. Your <radical>heart</radical> pounds beneath it, working overtime from the shock. What rushes between the two, in and out, is your <kanji>breath</kanji>.
k-breath.reading_mnemonic: Soku is the swimmer who comes up after far too long under and takes one enormous ragged gulp — 「<reading>そく</reading>」 — nose first, heart going like a hammer. That is what a breath you badly needed sounds like. そく.

k-daughter.meaning_mnemonic: A young <radical>woman</radical> reaches the door, ready to leave. A strict house rule ends up <radical>stopping</radical> her before nine. She sighs and stays inside, still somebody's <kanji>daughter</kanji>.
k-daughter.reading_mnemonic: Jou is how the neighbours refer to her, drawn out and a shade too formal — 「<reading>じょう</reading>」. It is the address for a girl of good family who is not allowed out tonight. She hears じょう and rolls her eyes.

k-daytime.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Daytime</kanji> is just the distance a <radical>ruler</radical> measures upward from the <radical>daybreak</radical> line to wherever the sun has climbed by now.
k-daytime.reading_mnemonic: Chuu, the loyal mouse with the tiny topknot, guards the sundial for the whole bright stretch of the day. When the shadow shrinks to nothing, he marks the middle of it with one proud <reading>ちゅう</reading>. That squeak is really just him biting a rice cracker, a single loud <reading>chew</reading>.

k-doctor.meaning_mnemonic: Whoever pulls the <radical>arrow</radical> out of you and shuts it inside a <radical>hiding enclosure</radical> has done a <kanji>doctor</kanji>'s entire job.
k-doctor.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail a hiker catches a stray arrow graze, and the doctor in the group digs a first-aid kit out of her pack. The moment the antiseptic touches the cut the hiker yelps a sharp <reading>eek</reading>, and it echoes off the rocks as <reading>い</reading>.

k-end.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the <radical>tree</radical>: a <radical>stick</radical> straight up, branches <radical>split</radical> aside. A <radical>lid</radical> stroke lies atop, longer than the <radical>one</radical> below — the twig's last inch: the <kanji>end</kanji>.
k-end.reading_mnemonic: Matsu is the woodsman who only ever takes the tip. He climbs the whole tree, snips the last bud off the top of it, and calls down 「<reading>まつ</reading>」 to say he has got there. まつ means there is nothing above him.

k-evening.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>evening</radical> radical you already learned and the <kanji>evening</kanji> kanji are the same character, so knowing your radicals cold just handed you this one for free.
k-evening.reading_mnemonic: The shrine sweeper <reading>Seki</reading> clocks in at exactly 「<reading>せき</reading>」 past sunset, never a minute early, so her entire shift is one long <kanji>evening</kanji> of shooing cats off the mossy steps.

k-father.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>father</radical> radical and the <kanji>father</kanji> kanji are the exact same shape and the same word, so this one comes free.
k-father.reading_mnemonic: Your father stands over the barbecue for a whole hot hour, and when the last plate is full he drops into a chair with a long <reading>ふ</reading> of relief. It is the exact sound a worn-out dad makes, a slow <reading>phew</reading> pushed out through the smoke. The kids know that breath means dinner is finally served.

k-friend.meaning_mnemonic: One stroke <radical>slides</radical> down from the top left across a bar of <radical>ground</radical>, met by a <radical>right hand</radical> rising underneath. Two hands close on each other, nobody paid, nobody in charge: that is a <kanji>friend</kanji>.
k-friend.reading_mnemonic: Yuu is always there before you, hand already out. He draws the greeting into a long two-beat call across the car park — 「<reading>ゆう</reading>」 — before you have shut the car door. ゆう means somebody is glad to see you.

k-gone.meaning_mnemonic: A mound of <radical>earth</radical> sits on top, underneath a sealed <radical>cocoon</radical> tucked out of sight. Whatever was inside wrapped up and went under the soil. Dig the mound over: nothing is left. It is <kanji>gone</kanji>.
k-gone.reading_mnemonic: Kyo is the magician who buries things and cannot get them back. He taps the mound, says 「<reading>きょ</reading>」 with a flourish, and that is genuinely the end of the trick. No reappearance, no second half. きょ, and it is gone.

k-he.meaning_mnemonic: A single <radical>step</radical> at the left edge, beside a hide hauled off in one sheet — all <radical>skin</radical>, no animal left. Someone walked past carrying it and is already down the road. That man you point at and cannot name: <kanji>he</kanji>.
k-he.reading_mnemonic: Hii is the little intake of breath you make when the man in the skin cloak goes past without a word — 「<reading>ひ</reading>」. By the time you finish it, he is round the corner. Every time you catch sight of him: ひ.

k-heart.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>wide box</radical> of a room, shoved to the back with <radical>rice</radical> and something <radical>big</radical> on top. You walk through every room to reach it; nobody outside the family does. The deepest room is the <kanji>heart</kanji>.
k-heart.reading_mnemonic: Ou is the grandmother who lives in that back room and has not come out in years. Knock and you get one long syllable through the paper door — 「<reading>おう</reading>」 — meaning she heard you and no, you may not come in. おう, from the very back of the house.

k-husband.meaning_mnemonic: Take the <radical>big</radical> figure — the <radical>person</radical> with arms flung wide. Lay one bar on top like a <radical>lid</radical>, so <radical>two</radical> strokes sit there, not one: his topknot pin. Grown and married: <kanji>husband</kanji>.
k-husband.reading_mnemonic: Fu is the same breath out through the nose you learned from his father, inherited exactly — arms folded in the doorway, one 「<reading>ふ</reading>」, no further comment offered. Getting married did not change it in the slightest.

k-me.meaning_mnemonic: Deep in a <radical>thicket</radical> where every other <radical>person</radical> is hidden, the only one I can still point to is <kanji>me</kanji>.
k-me.reading_mnemonic: Lost in that same thicket, a hiker finally crashes out into the open, hugging one soggy paperback <reading>book</reading> to his chest. When the ranger asks whose it is, all he can gasp between breaths is <reading>ぼく</reading> — mine, that one is me.
k-me.description: As a first-person word this is used mainly by boys and men and stays casual, so it is out of place in formal writing or when you must be very polite. It grew out of an older, humble word for a servant.

k-mister.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>official</radical> whose <radical>mouth</radical> is always hanging open to bark one more order is exactly the man everyone is forced to call <kanji>mister</kanji>.
k-mister.reading_mnemonic: That same barking official trudges up the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine. The cats swarm him and web him into a fat silk <reading>cocoon</reading> in seconds, and every command he keeps shouting from inside now comes out as a muffled <reading>くん</reading>.
k-mister.description: Not a polite title. As a name-suffix it marks a junior, a classmate, or a young man rather than a superior. As a stand-alone word it is a familiar 'you' that can sound blunt with someone you barely know.

k-morning.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Morning</kanji> is the one stretch of the day when the striped light of <radical>sunrise</radical> is already up while the <radical>moon</radical> still hangs in the window.
k-morning.reading_mnemonic: Cho, the rooster who always oversleeps, finally crows <reading>ちょう</reading> from the fence rail just as the last of the moonlight fades. Every house on the mountain trail wakes to that one lazy <reading>Cho</reading>. It is the sound that tells you the day has already started.
k-morning.description: Beyond the daily sense, 朝 also names a dynasty or imperial court, and it turns up in words for a ruling era or reigning house. At this level only morning is tested.

k-mother.meaning_mnemonic: You already know the <radical>mother</radical> radical, so this <kanji>mother</kanji> kanji is a gift, the same seated figure with both children held tight.
k-mother.reading_mnemonic: A mother <reading>boa</reading> has coiled around her eggs on the mossy shrine steps, guarding them with no patience at all. Each time a shrine cat pads too close she lifts her head and gives one low, flat note, <reading>ぼ</reading>. The cats have learned that a mother's warning means back off.

k-night.meaning_mnemonic: Once the last <radical>person</radical> outdoors presses a <radical>lid</radical> down over the fading <radical>evening</radical>, not one <radical>drop</radical> of light escapes, and the sealed black that follows is <kanji>night</kanji>.
k-night.reading_mnemonic: The guard on the late shift, <reading>Yah</reading>, is down to a single flat 「<reading>や</reading>」 by the time <kanji>night</kanji> falls, because twelve hours on his feet in the dark have scraped every other word out of him.

k-nightfall.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> on the left has been let off: the shape on the right squeezes from under the heavy lid, walking off <radical>exempt</radical>. Its shift is done; it drops below the roofline unbid. The sun excused from duty: <kanji>nightfall</kanji>.
k-nightfall.reading_mnemonic: Ban is the night watchman who takes over the moment the sun clocks off. He drags the gate shut and announces himself to the empty street — 「<reading>ばん</reading>」 — one flat syllable, every night, so you know the day is closed.

k-on-foot.meaning_mnemonic: A single <radical>step</radical> turns into a wild <radical>run</radical> down the road. There is no horse or cart anywhere in sight. So the whole trip happens <kanji>on foot</kanji>.
k-on-foot.reading_mnemonic: Toto the door-to-door turtle has never once taken a ride. He carries the sample doors on his shell and walks the entire round, and he announces himself at every house with the same syllable before he knocks — 「<reading>と</reading>」. と, and another mile.

k-private.meaning_mnemonic: A stalk of <radical>grain</radical> leans on the left, tucked behind it a little <radical>cocoon</radical>, sealed tight. Nobody else knows it is there. You grew the crop in the open, then kept one seed back for yourself: <kanji>private</kanji>.
k-private.reading_mnemonic: Shi is the quiet one who keeps her own small field behind the house, and when anyone asks what she is growing in it she says 「<reading>し</reading>」 and closes the gate. Not rude, exactly. Whatever is in there is hers, and し is the only answer you are ever going to get.

k-second-1.meaning_mnemonic: A stalk of <radical>grain</radical> stands in the field, thin at the very top. Someone plucks the <radical>small</radical> piece from its tip. That tiny sliver of time becomes one <kanji>second</kanji>.
k-second-1.reading_mnemonic: Byou is the hospital timekeeper with the stopwatch, and she counts out loud in a flat clipped bark — 「<reading>びょう</reading>」, びょう, びょう — one for every tick. She will not speed up and she will not stop. びょう is a single second landing.

k-submit.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> on the left; on the right <radical>two</radical> bars over <radical>ground</radical>, each on a <radical>stick</radical>, <radical>split</radical> into legs at the foot. A tray, lifted with both hands for somebody above to take: to <kanji>submit</kanji> a thing.
k-submit.reading_mnemonic: Kyou is the offering-bearer who never lowers the tray. He walks the entire length of the hall with it over his head, announcing himself at every pillar — 「<reading>きょう</reading>」 — until somebody finally takes the weight off him.

k-uncle.meaning_mnemonic: A stick of <radical>divination</radical> in the corner, a <radical>small</radical> mark beside it, a <radical>right hand</radical> scooping both up. He is the younger brother: not head of the family, so he gets the small share. Your <kanji>uncle</kanji>.
k-uncle.reading_mnemonic: Shuku is that uncle, and he arrives every year with the same trick. He shuffles the sticks, throws them down, sucks his teeth, and pronounces 「<reading>しゅく</reading>」 as though it settles the matter. Nobody knows what しゅく means. He will not explain.

k-what.meaning_mnemonic: Faced with a <radical>person</radical> who swears they <radical>can</radical> do absolutely anything, the only question left to ask is <kanji>what</kanji>.
k-what.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, perches on the power line outside Koichi's konbini and brags he can fix any broken machine. You point at the smoking till and ask <reading>か</reading>, meaning which part is even fixable. He just puffs a little flame and gives his only reply, a flat <reading>caw</reading>.

k-who.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Words</radical> stand on the left, on the right an <radical>old bird</radical> with its head cocked, waiting. You have talked for ten minutes and the bird still cannot tell which person you mean. It asks the only question left: <kanji>who</kanji>?
k-who.reading_mnemonic: Sui is the owl who works the gate. She leans down, blinks once, and hoots 「<reading>すい</reading>」, which in owl means name, please. Nobody gets past her without answering it. すい, すい, until you say who you are.

k-wife.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> sweeps her yard with a <radical>broom</radical> tied to a <radical>stick</radical>. She works until the bare <radical>ground</radical> is spotless. The neighbors call her the tidy <kanji>wife</kanji> of the house.
k-wife.reading_mnemonic: Sai is the one who actually decides. Ask her husband anything and he glances sideways at her first; she gives one flat 「<reading>さい</reading>」 and that is the answer on behalf of both of them. さい settles it.

k-yesterday.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> on the left, a <radical>stick</radical> upright on the right with one <radical>slide</radical> of a stroke off it. That stick is a sundial, its shadow scratched beside. The sun moved on; the mark left behind is <kanji>yesterday</kanji>.
k-yesterday.reading_mnemonic: Saku is the old gardener who checks his shadow-stick every dawn and then grumbles about how much better the light was 「<reading>さく</reading>」 — his one-word shorthand for the day before. Nothing is ever as good as さく was.

k-zero.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> kneels on the wet <radical>ground</radical> as <radical>rain</radical> pours down. A clerk presses his <radical>stamp</radical> on the puddle, and the ink washes away. Nothing is left to count, so he writes <kanji>zero</kanji>.
k-zero.reading_mnemonic: Rei is that clerk. She is scrupulously polite about it — a small bow, a murmured 「<reading>れい</reading>」 — and then she inks the nothing into your row and moves down the line. れい, bow, zero. She has done it forty times today.

k-employee.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>employee</kanji> is just one more <radical>mouth</radical> the company has to feed with its own <radical>money</radical>.
k-employee.reading_mnemonic: The gatekeeper is a retired innkeeper everyone calls <reading>Inn</reading>. She grunts <reading>いん</reading> every time she stamps a badge — one grunt per hire. By dusk, her voice is gone from saying it all day.
k-employee.description: 員 rarely stands alone as a word for 'employee' — it is a suffix meaning roughly 'a person belonging to,' always riding on a job title, company, or club, closer to '-er' than to a stand-alone noun.

k-tooth.meaning_mnemonic: Grains of <radical>rice</radical> that <radical>stop</radical> inside the <radical>open box</radical> of your jaw were caught there by one <kanji>tooth</kanji>.
k-tooth.reading_mnemonic: One shrine cat, nicknamed <reading>Shii</reading> for the hiss she makes mid-gnaw, clamps onto the bell rim and hisses <reading>し</reading> through the gap where a tooth used to be.

k-body.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>body</kanji> is the single <radical>book</radical> every <radical>person</radical> is born already holding and can never put down, since each fresh ache is one more page turning itself.
k-body.reading_mnemonic: No one warns you that the tailor <reading>Ty</reading> stitches the jacket straight onto your <kanji>body</kanji>, so you only notice when he yanks a seam tight against your ribs and mutters 「<reading>たい</reading>」.

k-thing.meaning_mnemonic: On the farm only the <radical>cow</radical> gets a real name, so every other object that is <radical>not</radical> her is written off as a plain <kanji>thing</kanji>.
k-thing.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Boots</reading> the sulky mailman kicks every loose <kanji>thing</kanji> off the path and spits 「<reading>ぶつ</reading>」 at each one he sends flying.

k-meal.meaning_mnemonic: When you quit cooking <radical>food (left)</radical> and do the exact <radical>opposite</radical>, you finally sit down to a proper <kanji>meal</kanji>.
k-meal.reading_mnemonic: A <kanji>meal</kanji> from <reading>Han</reading> always turns up sliced straight down the middle, because he cannot say 「<reading>はん</reading>」 without halving whatever sits on your plate.

k-tea.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole character as a steaming cup: delicate <radical>grass</radical> leaves curling up top like visible steam, a little <radical>person</radical> warming his hands round a <radical>tree</radical>-carved cup below. That curling steam over the cup is the whole picture: <kanji>tea</kanji>.
k-tea.reading_mnemonic: A dance instructor spins through the tearoom mid cha-cha lesson, a full teacup balanced on his palm. He counts the beat out loud — 「<reading>ちゃ</reading>」-cha-cha — until the cup tips and the lesson ends the same soaked way every time.

k-hit.meaning_mnemonic: Aim a pig's <radical>snout</radical> at one <radical>small</radical> coin in the dirt and it roots over and <kanji>hit</kanji>s the coin dead center every time.
k-hit.reading_mnemonic: Delivery runner <reading>Toe</reading> shouts 「<reading>とう</reading>」 every time a doorframe <kanji>hit</kanji>s him in the face, and at his sprint that is roughly once a second.

k-ill.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>ill</kanji> body is just a healthy one that <radical>sickness</radical> has bumped down to <radical>third class</radical>.
k-ill.reading_mnemonic: A mangy owl called <reading>Bee-Owl</reading> is so <kanji>ill</kanji> it can no longer hoot, and every 「<reading>びょう</reading>」 it coughs up costs it another feather.

k-section.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 部 as a squat filing cabinet: a <radical>stand</radical> strut over a slot like an open <radical>mouth</radical>, beside a little <radical>village</radical> of drawers. A clerk yanks the wrong drawer, gets buried in someone else's forms, and slams shut the one marked for his own <kanji>section</kanji>.
k-section.reading_mnemonic: A moth called <reading>Bu</reading> gets shut inside that same drawer overnight and beats its wings against the forms, the frantic drumming going <reading>ぶ</reading>, <reading>ぶ</reading>, <reading>ぶ</reading>, until dawn finally opens the drawer and lets it stagger free.

k-pedestal.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 台 as a squat stone pedestal: a <radical>cocoon</radical>-shaped knob on top, over a wide <radical>mouth</radical> of a base bolted to the ground. Workers winch a bronze statue onto it, and the block doesn't budge under the weight: solid, built for holding something up — a <kanji>pedestal</kanji>.
k-pedestal.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Dai</reading>, the giant baby, climbs onto that same pedestal to pose like a statue. One stomp cracks the stone with a boom that rattles windows, and he wails <reading>だい</reading>, <reading>だい</reading> as the block crumbles beneath him.

k-courtyard.meaning_mnemonic: The open ground between the <radical>shelter</radical> and the <radical>courts</radical> is the <kanji>courtyard</kanji> everybody has to cross.
k-courtyard.reading_mnemonic: The groundskeeper, named <reading>Tei</reading>, sprints after the goat squatting in the courtyard, tripping over the raked gravel and yelling <reading>てい</reading>, <reading>てい</reading> with every failed lunge, gravel spraying across the whole swept quiet.

k-turn.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 番 as a ticket dispenser bolted to a wall, its slots ruled like a tiny <radical>rice field</radical>, spitting out numbered slips kept strictly <radical>separate</radical>. Customers file into line by number, nobody out of place: the pure order of your <kanji>turn</kanji>.
k-turn.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a guard named <reading>Ban</reading> slams a wooden stamp onto the counter each time a new number is called. The crack echoes <reading>ばん</reading> through the shop as the line shuffles forward, one turn at a time.

k-empty.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>cave</radical> that a whole <radical>construction</radical> crew has finished digging out is, for all that effort, still just an <kanji>empty</kanji> hollow in the hill.
k-empty.reading_mnemonic: The pigeon <reading>Coo</reading> will only settle somewhere <kanji>empty</kanji>, because he needs the bare walls to bounce his proud 「<reading>くう</reading>」 back at him.

k-brush-stroke.meaning_mnemonic: One line dragged over flat <radical>ground</radical> is just a mark until an <radical>open box</radical> frames it, which is the entire <radical>reason</radical> it now reads as a deliberate <kanji>brush-stroke</kanji>.
k-brush-stroke.reading_mnemonic: The painter <reading>Gar</reading> grunts 「<reading>が</reading>」 on every single <kanji>brush-stroke</kanji>, so a busy afternoon of work leaves him too hoarse to speak.

k-reflect.meaning_mnemonic: When the <radical>sun</radical> sits at the exact <radical>center</radical> of the sky, the water below throws back its clearest <kanji>reflect</kanji>ion.
k-reflect.reading_mnemonic: Startled by his own doubled face in the water, the fisherman yelps 「<reading>Ay</reading>」 — 「<reading>えい</reading>」. The river throws the sound straight back at him a beat later, flat and unbothered, same as it did with the light.

k-roof.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>roof</kanji> is nothing but a sagging <radical>body</radical> sprawled overhead, and you only notice it the moment you <radical>arrive</radical> under it out of the rain.
k-roof.reading_mnemonic: The carpenter <reading>Oak</reading> turns down every job except a <kanji>roof</kanji>, and he barks 「<reading>おく</reading>」 down at you from the ridge beam the whole time he nails it on.

k-inst.meaning_mnemonic: Raise a truly <radical>perfect</radical> hall high on its own <radical>hill (left)</radical>, and it is grand enough to be called an <kanji>Inst.</kanji>
k-inst.reading_mnemonic: The keeper of the world's biggest <reading>inn</reading> keeps adding wings and halls, yet still bellows 「<reading>いん</reading>」 across a courtyard that has swollen into a full <kanji>Inst.</kanji>
k-inst.description: Short for institution: it names big establishments such as hospitals, temples, and government bodies, and rarely stands alone.

k-bureau.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>body</radical> that answers every <radical>phrase</radical> you say with another form to fill in is working in a <kanji>bureau</kanji>.
k-bureau.reading_mnemonic: Wedged into that same booth, a customer three forms deep chokes on chalky bureau dust drifting off the tax stacks, coughing out something between a wheeze and <reading>きょく</reading>. Koichi just nods, because everyone who reaches window three sounds exactly like they're trying to say <reading>choke</reading>.

k-convenience.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> who can <radical>renew</radical> anything for you without leaving the counter is selling pure <kanji>convenience</kanji>.
k-convenience.reading_mnemonic: The badger's slam sends the vending machine's change chute rattling out coins. The hiker who planned to buy one — a guy named <reading>Ben</reading> — just mutters 「<reading>べん</reading>」 under his breath, resigned to waiting outside in the rain.

k-building.meaning_mnemonic: Any <kanji>building</kanji> is just an empty shell until a <radical>bureaucrat</radical> moves in with his stamp and there is enough <radical>food (left)</radical> over from lunch to keep him at the desk.
k-building.reading_mnemonic: The night caretaker <reading>Khan</reading> looks after exactly one <kanji>building</kanji>, and he snaps 「<reading>かん</reading>」 at anyone who so much as leans on its door after closing.

k-near.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 近 as a signpost arrow, chopped short by an <radical>axe</radical>, that curled back along the <radical>road</radical> to jab at your own boots. On the mountain trail, the vending machine you swore was another hour up turns out one switchback away: <kanji>near</kanji>.
k-near.reading_mnemonic: At that vending machine, the hiker's little brother — pure <reading>kin</reading>, tagging along everywhere — presses his face to the glass and chants the machine's name like a drumbeat: <reading>きん</reading>. He is always, always this close.

k-slow.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>sheep</radical> dragging its whole <radical>body</radical> up the <radical>road</radical> makes every journey behind it <kanji>slow</kanji>.
k-slow.reading_mnemonic: The class hamster, <reading>Chi</reading>, is let loose to race him and loses on purpose, wheezing one flat unimpressed <reading>ち</reading> at the finish line — same track, same dragging in dead last.

k-walk.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>walk</kanji> is slow travel where your feet <radical>stop</radical> flat on the ground so often that you cover only a <radical>few</radical> steps a minute.
k-walk.reading_mnemonic: On the steep mountain trail, Grandma Kane climbs one slow step at a time, leaning her full weight on an old garden <reading>hoe</reading> and grunting <reading>ほ</reading> each time a foot lands flat. At this rate the vending machine at the top is an hour off, but she plants the hoe and takes the next step anyway.

k-mask.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>mask</radical> radical and the <kanji>mask</kanji> kanji are the same, and since a mask is only a face you can take off, the character also means the face or features behind it.
k-mask.reading_mnemonic: Menzo the actor wears a <kanji>mask</kanji> for every role so that behind it he could be any of a hundred <reading>men</reading>, and he crows 「<reading>めん</reading>」 at anyone who claims to know which.

k-demolition.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>net</radical> of torn <radical>clothing</radical> and <radical>ten</radical> loads of <radical>earth</radical> is all that is left after a <kanji>demolition</kanji>.

k-bring-up.meaning_mnemonic: Keep a <radical>cocoon</radical> under a warm <radical>lid</radical> for a whole <radical>month</radical> and you will <kanji>bring up</kanji> something alive.
k-bring-up.reading_mnemonic: A tiny kid named <reading>Iku</reading> waters the sunflower every morning before the bell, chanting <reading>いく</reading>, いく, grow already — as if the word itself could drag the stalk taller.

k-drought.meaning_mnemonic: After enough <radical>sunrise</radical>s with nothing but dust underneath them, farmers <radical>beg</radical> for the end of the <kanji>drought</kanji>.
k-drought.reading_mnemonic: The same heron kicks an empty tin <reading>can</reading> across the cracked mud out of pure boredom. It rolls to a stop with a hollow <reading>かん</reading> — the only sound this drought-cracked riverbank makes all summer.

k-get-wet.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Water</radical> has never once stopped to <radical>demand</radical> permission before making you <kanji>get wet</kanji>.
k-get-wet.reading_mnemonic: Koichi mops the puddle, muttering <reading>じゅ</reading>, じゅ — it sounds exactly like the first syllable of <reading>juice</reading>, which is unfortunately also what the floor smells like now.
k-get-wet.description: This character mostly means plain physical wetness — rain, tears, sweat. The "make love" sense is idiomatic, from a fixed phrase for an intimate scene in film or drama. On its own as a verb, it almost always just means damp, not romance.

k-correct.meaning_mnemonic: Walk <radical>one</radical> straight line and <radical>stop</radical> exactly on the mark to be counted <kanji>correct</kanji>.
k-correct.reading_mnemonic: Back in the classroom, the teacher asks who stopped exactly on the line. Sei's hand shoots up before she finishes asking, and he answers with his own name like it settles it: <reading>Sei</reading>, <reading>せい</reading> — crisp, correct, a little too pleased with himself.

k-straightaway.meaning_mnemonic: Line a <radical>cross</radical>hair up on your <radical>eye</radical> and nothing in the room stays <radical>hidden</radical>, so you spot the exit <kanji>straightaway</kanji>.
k-straightaway.reading_mnemonic: Mechanic <reading>Chock</reading> yanks the wheel block, barks 「<reading>ちょく</reading>」, and the van rolls <kanji>straightaway</kanji> down the drive, dead straight and gone in a second.
k-straightaway.description: Straightaway covers two senses here: a straight, unbent line, and something done at once with no detour. It also colours words for being frank.

k-suffering.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Old</radical> dry <radical>grass</radical> is the only thing left to chew on, which is the plain taste of <kanji>suffering</kanji>.
k-suffering.reading_mnemonic: He doesn't groan, exactly — what comes out is a strangled little <reading>coo</reading>, like a dove that swallowed a coin. The cashier doesn't even look up. She's heard that same <reading>く</reading> from every unlucky customer who trusted that shelf after dark.

k-even.meaning_mnemonic: Lay a <radical>shield</radical> flat on the ground and its face gives you a surface that is perfectly <kanji>even</kanji>.
k-even.reading_mnemonic: A hiker drags himself into the clearing, drops his pack, and lets out one long <reading>hey</reading>. That flat exhale is exactly the sound of <reading>へい</reading>: level, calm, done.

k-clear-up.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> getting the sky back to <radical>blue-green</radical> is what it means for the weather to <kanji>clear up</kanji>.
k-clear-up.reading_mnemonic: As the sky clears, Sei's hand shoots up first as always, uniform spotless despite the mud. She announces it loud and smug: <reading>せい</reading> — like she's the one who <reading>said</reading> the sky would clear.

k-heat.meaning_mnemonic: Any <radical>art</radical> that needs a <radical>fire</radical> lit under it is really the art of controlling <kanji>heat</kanji>.
k-heat.reading_mnemonic: The clerk mopping her forehead at the register is nicknamed <reading>Netsu</reading> for it. Every time that wall of heat rolls out, she groans her own name, <reading>ねつ</reading>, dragging it out like wading through hot fishing nets.

k-negative.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Negative</kanji> is what one hard <radical>slash</radical> makes of the <radical>stick</radical> standing in the <radical>ground</radical> once even its last <radical>drop</radical> is wiped away.
k-negative.reading_mnemonic: A theatre critic named <reading>Foo</reading> dismisses every play with one bored puff of breath, 「<reading>ふ</reading>」, the sound everyone now uses for a <kanji>negative</kanji> verdict.
k-negative.description: Almost always a prefix: 不 flips the following word to its opposite, like English un- or non-, and rarely stands alone.

k-precipitous.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>assembly</radical> that has to be held halfway up a <radical>hill</radical> tells you the ground there is <kanji>precipitous</kanji>.
k-precipitous.reading_mnemonic: Guarding that narrow ledge is <reading>Ken</reading>, the shiba who never leaves his wall of antique swords. Every hiker who nears the edge gets one warning bark of <reading>けん</reading> before he bares a blade in his teeth.
k-precipitous.description: Beyond the literal steep-cliff picture, this kanji usually carries a broader sense of danger or risk in real vocabulary — insurance, adventure, hazard — rather than physical steepness itself.

k-seethe.meaning_mnemonic: Charge a <radical>dollar</radical> for one cup of <radical>water</radical> and watch the whole queue <kanji>seethe</kanji>.
k-seethe.reading_mnemonic: A jumpy regular named <reading>Futz</reading> keeps mashing the button, muttering <reading>ふつ</reading>, ふつ under his breath every time the noodle water surges past the rim. Say his nervous little ふつ ふつ and the reading is stuck in your head with the foam.

k-burn.meaning_mnemonic: Hold a match to it, the <radical>fire</radical> takes, and <radical>so it is</radical> settled that the whole thing will <kanji>burn</kanji>.
k-burn.reading_mnemonic: The neighborhood kids call Grandma Kane <reading>Nan</reading>, and when the incense flares she comes flying out stamping sparks off the mossy steps, yelling the cat's name so fast it comes out <reading>ねん</reading>. Picture Nan hollering ねん at that cat, and the reading burns itself in.

k-current.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Water</radical> that pulls a <radical>banner</radical> straight out downstream is showing you exactly where the <kanji>current</kanji> runs.
k-current.reading_mnemonic: A boy named <reading>Ryu</reading> wades out too far, and the current takes him too. His voice trails off in a long <reading>りゅう</reading> as he's carried past the reeds and around the bend.

k-times.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>mouth</radical> inside an <radical>enclosure</radical> saying the same thing over is how you count the <kanji>times</kanji> it happened.
k-times.reading_mnemonic: Sei's PE teacher, a man everyone calls <reading>Kai</reading>, stands at the gate barking a number each time a runner completes the loop: <reading>かい</reading>, かい, かい, one shout per lap. By the tenth lap nobody's counting anything but Kai's voice landing on かい.

k-surpass.meaning_mnemonic: A messenger who can <radical>run</radical> faster than the <radical>warrior</radical> chasing him will <kanji>surpass</kanji> him inside a mile.
k-surpass.reading_mnemonic: At the summit, a hiker named <reading>Etsu</reading> collapses against the vending machine and groans <reading>えつ</reading> between gasps — the same groan echoes down the trail every time someone else finally surpasses that last ridge.

k-traffic.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>walled path</radical> feeding onto one open <radical>road</radical> is where all of the <kanji>traffic</kanji> ends up.
k-traffic.reading_mnemonic: A hall monitor named <reading>Tsuu</reading> stands in the doorway blowing one note — <reading>つう</reading> — every few seconds, waving the flood of students through without ever telling them to stop. By the fortieth <reading>つう</reading> you can still hear it at home.

k-severance.meaning_mnemonic: Bringing an <radical>axe</radical> down on a standing bundle of <radical>rice</radical> stalks makes a very clean <kanji>severance</kanji>.
k-severance.reading_mnemonic: A fisherman named <reading>Dan</reading> stands at the riverbank when his line goes slack. He shouts <reading>だん</reading> — the exact sound of a taut line snapping in half, sharp and final.

k-help.meaning_mnemonic: One more pair of hands, and <radical>moreover</radical> all of their <radical>power</radical> as well, is what <kanji>help</kanji> actually means.
k-help.reading_mnemonic: Back on their feet, the rescued customer, who Koichi has started calling <reading>Jo</reading>, breathes out a long shaky <reading>じょ</reading>, half relief and half embarrassment, still clutching the onigiri that never hit the floor.

k-stubborn.meaning_mnemonic: Anybody who argues from the <radical>beginning</radical> using nothing but their own <radical>head</radical> is being <kanji>stubborn</kanji>.
k-stubborn.reading_mnemonic: Every time a hiker shoves the boulder, a hermit camped beside it cups his hands and grunts <reading>がん</reading> — the same flat sound, like someone saying <reading>gone</reading> through a clenched jaw. It's the only word he says. The boulder still hasn't moved.

k-accustomed.meaning_mnemonic: Let the same thing <radical>pierce</radical> your <radical>heart</radical> often enough and you will get <kanji>accustomed</kanji> to it.
k-accustomed.reading_mnemonic: Behind the counter, Koichi restocks the drink case so many times his hand does it alone — each can lands with a flat clink that sounds like <reading>かん</reading>, someone saying <reading>khan</reading> without the h. He's stopped hearing it. That's how accustomed he's become.

k-overdo.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>crooked mouth</radical> retelling the story the whole length of the <radical>road</radical> is certain to <kanji>overdo</kanji> it.
k-overdo.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow watches from the power line above the flooded bank. One puff of flame would do, but she can't stop — she keeps cawing <reading>か</reading>, <reading>か</reading>, like someone stuck repeating <reading>kah</reading>, torching the same branch long after it's ash.

k-period.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>That</radical> same <radical>moon</radical> coming round to where it started marks the end of one <kanji>period</kanji>.
k-period.reading_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit lives in the tree over Grandma Kane's shrine bell. Every time it rings she giggles <reading>き</reading>, <reading>き</reading> — like someone laughing the word <reading>key</reading>. She only laughs on the ring, never between, so her giggle marks that same fixed moment each time.

k-scold.meaning_mnemonic: One <radical>mouth</radical> going at you for the <radical>seven</radical>th time has stopped being advice and become a <kanji>scold</kanji>ing.
k-scold.reading_mnemonic: Back at the konbini, the clerk everyone calls <reading>Sheets</reading> is still rubbing his ear from the crack of the cane. Every time the till beeps near him now, he flinches and mutters <reading>しつ</reading> under his breath, bracing for another scolding.

k-praise.meaning_mnemonic: Wrapping somebody in fine <radical>clothing</radical> to <radical>protect</radical> them from criticism is one way to <kanji>praise</kanji> them.
k-praise.reading_mnemonic: The shrine's caretaker, nicknamed <reading>Whoa</reading> because it's the only thing she ever says, watches the bell hum with approval. She breathes out a satisfied <reading>ほう</reading>, her robe still settling.

k-apologize.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Words</radical> you <radical>shoot</radical> off before thinking are exactly the ones you have to <kanji>apologize</kanji> for later.
k-apologize.reading_mnemonic: The archer at the riverbank, a title everyone shortens to <reading>Shah</reading>, still cannot fire a straight shot. Every arrow that misses gets the same muttered <reading>しゃ</reading>, half apology, half excuse, as he bows and fishes it out of the reeds.
k-apologize.description: This kanji covers more than sorry: the same character also carries formal thanks and, in some compounds, an outright refusal or decline. Underneath all three is one idea, a formal spoken response rather than plain regret, so context decides whether it reads as apology, gratitude, or a firm no.

k-counter-for.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>bow</radical> strung for a <radical>long</radical> shot is the sort of thing you need a <kanji>counter for bows</kanji> to tally.
k-counter-for.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the trail, the hiker everyone calls <reading>Chow</reading> counts the taut bows by the vending machine. He taps each string and grunts <reading>ちょう</reading> under his breath — one, two, three.
k-counter-for.description: As a counter, this kanji counts things held taut by a string, such as bows and stringed instruments, not flat sheets or long thin objects, which take other counters. The verb sense stretch or spread is the same idea: pulling something tight, which is why the same character became the counting word for anything strung that way.

k-wait.meaning_mnemonic: Every <radical>step</radical> up to the <radical>Buddhist temple</radical> already has somebody standing on it, so you <kanji>wait</kanji>.
k-wait.reading_mnemonic: A hiker named Tai sits below the blocked switchback, stomach growling, dreaming only of <reading>Thai</reading> food waiting in the valley below. He mutters <reading>たい</reading>, <reading>たい</reading> under his breath, thinking of nothing else, until the boulder finally shifts and he can climb down to eat.

k-celebrate.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>cult</radical> and your <radical>elder brother</radical> finally agreeing on something is reason enough to <kanji>celebrate</kanji>.
k-celebrate.reading_mnemonic: The coach gets <reading>shook</reading> so hard by the shoulder-ride that his whistle flies into the bleachers. <reading>しゅく</reading>! <reading>しゅく</reading>! the players chant with every shake — and a second later, he tips backward into the equipment cart.

k-blessing.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>cult</radical> that promises <radical>to fill</radical> your storehouse by spring is selling you a <kanji>blessing</kanji>.
k-blessing.reading_mnemonic: The monk insists it isn't a <reading>fluke</reading>: that same shrine cat has picked the luckiest fortune four mornings running. <reading>ふく</reading>, he mutters, chalking another tally on the gate, certain the cat is hoarding it all for itself.

k-emotion.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>All</radical> of the <radical>heart</radical> arriving at once and none of the head arriving at all is <kanji>emotion</kanji>.
k-emotion.reading_mnemonic: His friend picks up the crushed <reading>can</reading> and turns it over in her hands — even the dent looks like it's crying. <reading>かん</reading>, she says, tapping the metal, and that flat little sound is the whole moment collapsing.

k-hang.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>hand</radical> nailing an <radical>omen</radical> to the door is going to <kanji>hang</kanji> it where everybody has to look.
k-hang.reading_mnemonic: Kaa lands on that same hook, tilts his head at the empty <reading>sky</reading>, and screeches <reading>かい</reading> at the swinging poncho. It's the same rasp he gives anything left dangling in his sightline.

k-propose.meaning_mnemonic: Getting your <radical>hand</radical> up at the <radical>right</radical> moment is the whole skill of knowing how to <kanji>propose</kanji> something.
k-propose.reading_mnemonic: Tei, a deer too formal for the konbini, holds an empty tray at arm's length over that same counter like he's presenting a proposal, and repeats <reading>てい</reading>, <reading>tray</reading>, until someone puts something on it. Nobody ever does; he holds the pose anyway.

k-nonplussed.meaning_mnemonic: Being handed <radical>three</radical> <radical>big</radical> silk <radical>cocoon</radical>s with no explanation at all leaves anybody <kanji>nonplussed</kanji>.
k-nonplussed.reading_mnemonic: The bell's still ringing when the <reading>sun</reading> clears the shrine roof and floods the steps with light. The cat squints up at it, hisses one flat <reading>さん</reading>, and doesn't move an inch.
k-nonplussed.description: 参 splits between two senses. As the humble verb 参る it means to go or come. On its own or in compounds it instead carries nonplussed, worn out, at your wit's end. The shape doesn't distinguish them; only the sentence does.

k-have-the.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>stick</radical> raised up into the <radical>sun</radical> is the old signal that you <kanji>have the honor to</kanji> speak next.
k-have-the.reading_mnemonic: Shin catches the arrow's fletching on his <reading>shin</reading> as it flies past the same target, yelps <reading>しん</reading>, and doubles over clutching his shin — still bowing out of habit as he hops on one foot.
k-have-the.description: 申 covers three unrelated uses. As 申す, humble language for say, it gives have the honor to. On its own it also names the monkey sign of the zodiac, and the old two-hour block from 3 to 5PM. Only context tells you which sense you're reading.

k-return.meaning_mnemonic: Turn round and take the <radical>opposite</radical> <radical>road</radical> back the way you came to <kanji>return</kanji>.
k-return.reading_mnemonic: That startled hen at the summit vending machine won't shut up about it. Every time the boomerang whips past, she screeches <reading>へん</reading>, like a slapstick chicken shouting <reading>hen</reading>.

k-take-along.meaning_mnemonic: On the riverbank you tie a string of tin cans to the back of a toy <radical>vehicle</radical> and drag it down the muddy <radical>road</radical>. A wren, a bucket, and someone's lost sandal all snag onto the string, towed helplessly in a rattling line behind you. Everything hooked and <kanji>taken along</kanji>.
k-take-along.reading_mnemonic: The wren tangled in the string won't stop singing about it, chirping <reading>れん</reading> in a tiny outraged voice. Every time the cart yanks the line taut, it's like it's shouting <reading>wren</reading> at the mud.

k-fit.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>One</radical> <radical>person</radical> and one <radical>mouth</radical> for every seat at the table is when the numbers finally <kanji>fit</kanji>.
k-fit.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's enormous shrine bell takes one clean hit and rings out a long <reading>ごう</reading>. It's the same low <reading>go</reading> tone the fitted rice cracker halves seem to hum back at each other.

k-make.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> with an <radical>abrupt</radical> idea at two in the morning gets straight up to <kanji>make</kanji> it.
k-make.reading_mnemonic: The onigiri-maker keeps losing his <reading>sock</reading> in the rice pile and swearing <reading>さく</reading> under his breath every time he digs another one out, sticky rice clinging to his toes.

k-insect.meaning_mnemonic: Anything small enough to get <radical>in</radical> through a shut window is almost certainly an <kanji>insect</kanji>.
k-insect.reading_mnemonic: Chuu the loyal mouse trails the beetle across the shrine steps, tiny topknot bobbing, and posts himself over its twitching antenna like an unassigned guard. Every twitch earns one crisp report — <reading>ちゅう</reading> — from the mouse everyone calls <reading>Chuu</reading>, guarding an insect nobody asked him to.

k-horse.meaning_mnemonic: Four legs pounding hard enough to strike <radical>fire</radical> off the stones belong to a <kanji>horse</kanji>.
k-horse.reading_mnemonic: Uncle Ba, the trail's sunburnt vending-machine repairman, trudges up to the fresh dent and sighs one flat <reading>ば</reading> — the same tired <reading>bah</reading> he lets out every time. The horse just watches, proud of the dent.

k-cow.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>cow</radical> radical you already know and the <kanji>cow</kanji> kanji are the exact same character, so this one is a free point for learning your radicals.
k-cow.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Gyoo</reading> the milkmaid wraps both arms around the <kanji>cow</kanji> and squeezes so hard that the startled animal wheezes 「<reading>ぎゅう</reading>」 and treads on her boot.

k-star.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>sun</radical> too far off to warm anything, with its own <radical>life</radical> still burning away, is a <kanji>star</kanji>.
k-star.reading_mnemonic: Sei, the star student, is first to point at it, hand shooting up before anyone else's, and announces it in one crisp syllable — <reading>せい</reading> — like she is always first to <reading>say</reading> the answer. The sports field goes quiet, impressed despite itself.

k-forest.meaning_mnemonic: One more <radical>tree</radical> than a <radical>grove</radical> can hold and you are standing in a <kanji>forest</kanji>.
k-forest.reading_mnemonic: Still on that same trail, a hiker named <reading>Shin</reading> refuses to admit he's lost among the fused trunks. He barks his shin on a hidden root and yelps <reading>しん</reading>, the sound echoing uselessly off the trunks, then keeps limping in circles.

k-grove.meaning_mnemonic: A second <radical>tree</radical> close enough to tangle branches with the first already counts as a <kanji>grove</kanji>.
k-grove.reading_mnemonic: A jogger named <reading>Rin</reading> ducks through that same gap every morning, and the small bell tied to one trunk swings with her stride, chiming <reading>りん</reading> with each step until she's through the gate.

k-pond.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Water</radical> that goes nowhere and curls back on itself like a <radical>snake tail</radical> is a <kanji>pond</kanji>.
k-pond.reading_mnemonic: A boy named <reading>Chi</reading> wades in after his shoe, ankle-deep, and yelps <reading>ち</reading> when something unseen brushes his foot in the murk, though he never actually finds out what it was.

k-boulder.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>stone</radical> that came off the <radical>mountain</radical> and is still bigger than your house is a <kanji>boulder</kanji>.
k-boulder.reading_mnemonic: A fisherman named <reading>Gan</reading> swings his rod back to cast and cracks it straight into that lump with a flat, ugly thud: <reading>がん</reading>. He stands there rubbing the crack in the wood — the rock doesn't chip.

k-seduce.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>mouth</radical> that can talk a drawn <radical>sword</radical> back into its sheath knows perfectly well how to <kanji>seduce</kanji>.
k-seduce.reading_mnemonic: Backstage, Sho takes his bow, and the crowd gasps <reading>しょう</reading> in unison — one long <reading>show</reading> of a breath. He tips his tiny top hat, and that gasp is the only applause a magician his size ever needs.

k-swim.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 泳 as one motion at the riverbank: an arm slices forward through the <radical>water</radical>. It flings a trail of <radical>drop</radical>lets out sideways behind it in one clean streak. That arm-cut trailing a spray of droplets is <kanji>swim</kanji> — caught mid-stroke, again and again.
k-swim.reading_mnemonic: At the same riverbank, the lifeguard Ei blows her whistle every single stroke you take, shouting <reading>えい</reading>! — <reading>Ay</reading>! — like she's counting each one out loud. By the tenth lap her voice is the only thing keeping your arms moving.

k-kill.meaning_mnemonic: You can <radical>mow</radical> with a <radical>tree</radical> branch if you have to, but the <radical>pike</radical> is the one built to <kanji>kill</kanji>.
k-kill.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a stray satsuma rolls off the offering tray and lands square on a fly mid-buzz — <reading>さつ</reading>, flat, gone, before the enormous bell even finishes ringing. The shrine cats stare at the <reading>satsuma</reading> like it just committed a crime.

k-take.meaning_mnemonic: Grabbing somebody by the <radical>ear</radical> with your <radical>right hand</radical> is the rudest way there is to <kanji>take</kanji> them anywhere.
k-take.reading_mnemonic: Same trail, one step later: Shu's <reading>shoe</reading> catches the vending machine's coin return and yanks out a whole handful of forgotten change. <reading>しゅ</reading>! he yelps, hopping on one foot, pockets suddenly heavier.

k-harmony.meaning_mnemonic: Enough <radical>grain</radical> for every <radical>mouth</radical> in the village buys a whole season of <kanji>harmony</kanji>.
k-harmony.reading_mnemonic: The shrine's droopy-eyed monk, Wah, startles awake for the bell and breathes out a long <reading>wah</reading> of relief once the cats settle down. That same <reading>わ</reading> drifts off the mossy steps every single morning.
k-harmony.description: 和 alone usually means harmony or peace, but as a prefix on other words it commonly means Japanese-style - Japanese food, a Japanese-style room - describing where something comes from rather than describing peacefulness itself.

k-pour.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Water</radical> for the <radical>lord</radical> is the one cup you never <kanji>pour</kanji> carelessly.
k-pour.reading_mnemonic: Chuu the mouse wades into the flooded furrows anyway, topknot dripping, refusing to abandon his post at the farmer's side. He squeaks a soggy salute, half sound half hiccup: <reading>chew</reading>, <reading>ちゅう</reading> - loyal even ankle-deep in the river the farmer just poured across the field.

k-plains.meaning_mnemonic: Land the <radical>village</radical> claimed <radical>beforehand</radical> and then never got round to fencing is still open <kanji>plains</kanji>.

k-park.meaning_mnemonic: A groundskeeper drapes a <radical>clothing</radical> sheet over the flowerbeds like a tent. k-angle.meaning_mnemonic: A carpenter drags his <radical>angle</radical> gauge to every crooked joint on a birdhouse. Thirty degrees here, ninety there, no two joints match. He shrugs and calls every mismatched joint a perfect <kanji>angle</kanji>.

k-meat.meaning_mnemonic: This is the <radical>meat</radical> radical and the <kanji>meat</kanji> kanji at once, one shape doing both jobs, so you already know it from the butcher's-shop window.

k-door.meaning_mnemonic: Toto the turtle sells a sample <radical>door</radical> that never stays shut. He chases it down every street as it swings open again and again. The whole town now knows him by that one runaway <kanji>door</kanji>.

k-autumn.meaning_mnemonic: A stalk of <radical>grain</radical> leans over and drops onto the <radical>fire</radical> burning beside the field. It catches fast and sends smoke drifting over the empty rows. That smoky smell means <kanji>autumn</kanji> has arrived.

k-feathers.meaning_mnemonic: A startled duck yanks out a <radical>feather</radical> and it drifts onto the pond. The wind tugs more loose until dozens follow it down. Soon the whole pond is coated in floating <kanji>feathers</kanji>.

k-bird.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>bird</radical> radical and the <kanji>bird</kanji> kanji are the same character, and it also means chicken, because a chicken is just the bird you are most likely to eat.

k-chirp.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>bird</radical> lands on the goalpost during recess. Its beak opens into a wide <radical>mouth</radical> like a square hole. Out comes a piercing <kanji>chirp</kanji> that stops the game.

k-ri.meaning_mnemonic: The furthest you can still make out a village by <radical>sun</radical>light is roughly one <kanji>ri</kanji>.
k-ri.reading_mnemonic: The village elder who waves hikers toward the paddies goes by <reading>Lee</reading>. Every exhausted hiker calls back a grateful <reading>り</reading> as thanks. That's as much of his name as anyone manages out of breath. He just nods toward the shade.

k-snow.meaning_mnemonic: The falling <radical>rain</radical> freezes solid before it lands outside the temple. A monk grabs a <radical>broom</radical> and sweeps the icy drops into soft white drifts. He won't ring the bell until every trace of <kanji>snow</kanji> is gone.

k-number.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> drops a bag of <radical>rice</radical> and grains spill everywhere. k-number.reading_mnemonic: Back in that gym, the scorekeeper — a woman named <reading>Sue</reading> — squints at the tally and groans <reading>すう</reading>, dragging the sound out like she dreads the total. The same scattered rice still crunches under her shoes.

k-summer.meaning_mnemonic: Your bare feet scorch on the baked <radical>ground</radical>. You point at <radical>self</radical> and swear the heat does not bother you. Then your <radical>trailing foot</radical> drags behind, and the stubborn heat becomes <kanji>summer</kanji>.

Too hot even for him, he cracks his beak and a weak puff of flame escapes with a scorched <reading>か</reading>. That tired flame-cough is how you remember summer's reading, <reading>か</reading>.

k-winter.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Winter</kanji> is the one season your <radical>trailing foot</radical> drags a strip of <radical>ice</radical> across the floor with every step you take indoors.

k-cloud.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Rain</radical> falls onto the <radical>ground</radical> where <radical>two</radical> silkworms spin themselves into a <radical>cocoon</radical>. The cocoon soaks up water until it swells and floats free. It drifts upward and puffs into a <kanji>cloud</kanji>.

k-face.meaning_mnemonic: Because a <radical>lad</radical> this vain only ever grooms the side of his <radical>head</radical> that people see, every hair on his <kanji>face</kanji> is perfect and the back is a mess.

k-springtime.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> steps onto the thawed <radical>ground</radical> after a long winter. k-lower.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> strides forward, then drops into a sudden crouch. They press their <radical>family name</radical> seal onto the <radical>ground</radical> instead of a desk. Bowing that low is what <kanji>lower</kanji> means.

k-public-chamber.description: This kanji almost never stands alone. In real use it is nearly always the second half of a compound naming one specific large room — a dining hall, a lecture hall — rather than a generic public chamber on its own.

k-research.meaning_mnemonic: You climb into a dark <radical>cave</radical> holding a hook bent like <radical>nine</radical>. You lower the hook and search along the floor for the bottom. Digging that deep for answers is called <kanji>research</kanji>.

k-ride.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>tree</radical> trunk with an angled <radical>chevron</radical> nailed on as a seat and a wad of <radical>grass</radical> for padding is the worst sled you will ever <kanji>ride</kanji>.

k-short.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>arrow</radical> hits a target and snaps in half, the pieces splitting apart like <radical>eight</radical>. k-short.description: Beyond literal shortness, 短 also carries the sense of a shortcoming. It's the kind of short that comes up when someone lists a personality flaw or weak point, not just a measurement of length.

k-silver.meaning_mnemonic: Workers stack bars of <radical>gold</radical> in the vault. The inspector's boot hits an immovable <radical>stopping</radical> point at one duller bar. She sets that reject aside and calls it <kanji>silver</kanji>.
k-silver.reading_mnemonic: The vault inspector introduces herself as <reading>Gin</reading>. She says it the same flat way every time she rejects a bar, <reading>ぎん</reading>, like she's already bored of the job. She's the one who decided, years ago, that silver deserved its own shelf.

k-sino.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Sino-</kanji> names the land where a <radical>husband</radical> farms the <radical>grass</radical> by the <radical>water</radical> and every <radical>mouth</radical> for miles drinks from that one river.
k-sino.reading_mnemonic: A loud warlord called <reading>Khan</reading> stamps 「<reading>かん</reading>」 on every scroll, teapot, and character that ever came out of China, so his one syllable is now the mark of anything <kanji>Sino-</kanji>.
k-sino.description: Sino- is the combining form of 'Chinese', and this kanji points to Han China in particular. In a few set compounds it instead means 'a man', often a rough one.

k-substitute.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> dreads standing guard all night at the <radical>ceremony</radical>. They stuff a coat with straw and lean it against the post instead. Nobody notices the swap, and the dummy becomes their <kanji>substitute</kanji>.
k-substitute.reading_mnemonic: Dai, the giant baby, truck-sized, toddles up and spots the straw double leaned against the post. He points and wails <reading>だい</reading>, landing like the English word <reading>dye</reading> spilled across the square. The ground trembles with every sob. The straw substitute never even flinches.

k-sultry.meaning_mnemonic: It turns <kanji>sultry</kanji> when <radical>someone</radical> is pinned in an open field and the <radical>sun</radical> bakes the damp air around them for hours.
k-sultry.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Show</reading> the weatherman does his forecast live from a treeless field, so overheated that the one syllable he can force out, 「<reading>しょ</reading>」, is now the station's official word for a <kanji>sultry</kanji> afternoon.
k-sultry.description: This is heat from the air or the weather, not from a hot object. Something hot to the touch, like a pan or a kettle, is written with another kanji entirely.

k-vegetable.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>vegetable</kanji> is the one leafy plant you <radical>pick</radical> out of a whole patch of <radical>grass</radical> and actually agree to eat.
k-vegetable.reading_mnemonic: Handed a dinner of nothing but boiled <kanji>vegetable</kanji>s, <reading>Sigh</reading> the grump slumps in his chair and lets out one long, defeated 「<reading>さい</reading>」.

k-ward.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>ward</kanji> is the slice of city the council <radical>mow</radical>s off and seals inside its own <radical>hiding enclosure</radical>, so tax collectors know whose doors to knock on.
k-ward.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Coo</reading> the pigeon patrols only her home <kanji>ward</kanji>, and the moment a stranger's shoe crosses the boundary she coos one furious 「<reading>く</reading>」 and waddles back.
